SOURCE: "The Leaderboard Illusion", Shivalika Singh, Yiyang Nan, Alex Wang, Daniel D'souza, Sayash Kapoor, Ahmet Üstün, Sanmi Koyejo, Yuntian Deng, Shayne Longpre, Noah A. Smith, Beyza Ermis, Marzieh Fadaee, Sara Hooker (Cohere Labs, Cohere, Princeton, Stanford, Waterloo, MIT, AI2, UW). Venue as printed: none. The PDF says "Released as a preprint on May 13, 2025" and "arXiv:2504.20879v2 [cs.AI] 12 May 2025". Treat as preprint, 2025.

COVERAGE: 72 of 72 pages extracted (187,135 chars). Read in full: pp. 1-31 (body, limitations, related work, conclusion) and pp. 42-47, 65-72 (appendices A-D, E intro, F-M). Skimmed only: references pp. 31-42. Sampled, not read line by line: pp. 48-64, Tables 2-5 (lists of private and public model names, model self-identification responses, per-model sampling rates). No per-row claim from those tables is reported below.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: Two identical checkpoints submitted to the Arena got different scores, so publishing only the better one inflates a score with no quality difference.
  number: 1052 vs 1069; 4 models ranked between them
  setup: real Arena (vision leaderboard) experiment, Aya-Vision-8B, two identical variants, March 2025, n = 1 pair
  quote: "notable differences in final Arena scores between identical checkpoints: 1052 (±21/22) and 1069 (±19/23). As a result, 4 models are positioned between our two identical checkpoints."
  where: p. 15

- claim: Two near-final variants of one model differed by 38 points.
  number: 1097 vs 1059; 9 models in between
  setup: real Arena, two Aya-Vision-32B variants, n = 1 pair
  quote: "(1097 (±29/25) vs. 1059 (±18/23)), with 9 models falling in between both variants"
  where: p. 15

- claim: Best-of-N selection is biased upward by construction, and the bias grows with N.
  number: about +50 points at N = 20 (simulation); analytic 17.7 points for identical variants at N = 50; about 56 with true spread of 20
  setup: simulation, variant family with latent mean score 1200, Bradley-Terry fit with bootstrap; analytic case assumes n = 3,000 votes, Gaussian noise, equal-strength matches
  quote: "testing just 20 variants yields a notable increase of approximately 50 points in the maximum score identified"; "bias ≈ 6.34 √2 ln 50 = 17.7 Arena Score"; "σtrue = 20 Arena Score yields bias ≈ 56 Arena Score at N = 50, n = 3 000"
  where: pp. 13, 67, 69

- claim: Some providers tested many private variants before release.
  number: Meta 27, Google 10 (main leaderboard); Meta 43 including vision
  setup: authors' scrape of 5,864 battles, January-March 2025; provider attributed from model self-identification
  quote: "Meta and Google had the most active private models during this period, with 27 and 10 models, respectively."
  where: p. 10

- claim: Training on Arena data raises in-distribution win rate and does not raise MMLU.
  number: win rate 23.5% -> 42.7% -> 49.9% (relative +112.3%); MMLU 66.5%, 64.4%, 65.9%
  setup: 7B Cohere base model, 0/30/70% arena data in the fine-tuning mix, 1.3K steps, batch 128, no tuning; 500 English ArenaHard prompts vs Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, judged by gpt-4o-2024-11-20 (not human votes)
  quote: "The relative gains in win-rates are 81.7% for the 30_arena and 112.3% for the 70_arena variant."; "MMLU performance slightly declined from 66.5% (0_arena) to 64.4% (30_arena) and 65.9% (70_arena)"
  where: pp. 20-21, 72

- claim: Data access is concentrated in a few providers.
  number: Google 19.2%, OpenAI 20.4%; 83 open-weight models 29.7%; 41 open-source models 8.9%; proprietary 61.4%
  setup: estimated from share of battles in leaderboard snapshots, January 2024-April 2025, 243 models, 42 providers
  quote: "Google and OpenAI have received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of all data on the arena, respectively. In contrast, a combined 83 open-weight models have only received an estimated 29.7% of the total data."
  where: p. 1

- claim: Sampling rates differ about tenfold across providers.
  number: 34% max daily (Google, OpenAI) vs 3.3% (Reka)
  setup: scraped sample, January-March 2025, about 150 battles a day, so daily rates rest on small counts
  quote: "Google and OpenAI reach a maximum daily sampling rate of 34%, while Reka registers the lowest at 3.3%."
  where: p. 16

- claim: The test set repeats itself month to month.
  number: 20.14% average loss on de-duplication, peak 26.5%; 7.3% exact cross-month repeats, 9% by embedding similarity
  setup: 197,217 single-turn prompts received through Cohere's API, November 2024-April 2025 (February excluded); Cohere models only
  quote: "de-duplication resulted in an average prompt loss of 20.14%, peaking at 26.5% in March 2025"; "7.3% of prompts from December 2024 appear again in the exact form in January 2025."
  where: p. 19

- claim: Most public models are no longer sampled, and deprecation can break Bradley-Terry assumptions.
  number: 205 of 243 silently deprecated vs 47 official; 87.8% open-weight, 89% open-source, 80% proprietary
  setup: "silent" defined as an average of 10 or fewer battles, March 3-April 23, 2025; the ranking effect is shown only in toy simulations (4 and 7 models, 2,000 battles)
  quote: "Of the 243 public models, 205 participated in an average of 10 or fewer battles during this period"
  where: pp. 69, 21

LIMITS
- Authors concede: no access to raw Arena data; scrape covers only January-March 2025, coinciding with the Llama 4 launch; provider attribution from self-identification is "inherently approximate" (14 private models unattributed); adversarial voting not studied.
- Not shown: no observed scores for other providers' private variants, so no measured inflation of any published rank. The real-world evidence is two pairs of the authors' own models. The reported intervals of the identical pair overlap, and no significance test is given.
- Deprecation and sparsity harms are simulated, not measured on Arena data.
- Overfitting result uses an LLM judge on ArenaHard, one model size, three runs, a proprietary training mix.
- Conflict of interest, disclosed: authors are largely Cohere and submitted models to the Arena.
- Dated: policies and figures are as of April 2025. No Arena response is included.

BUILDS ON: Bradley & Terry (1952); Chiang et al. (2024) for Chatbot Arena and its active sampling rule; Ford Jr (1957) for graph connectivity; Arnold et al. (1992) and David & Nagaraja (2003) for order statistics; Li et al. (2024c) for ArenaHard; Boubdir et al. (2024) on Elo; Goodhart's law as framing.

CODE: none. Formulas worth keeping: "Arena Score = 1000 + 400 ln 10 β̂" (garbled in extraction, p. 66); standard error on the Arena scale ≈ 347.4/√n (p. 67); bias(N, n, σtrue) = sqrt(σtrue² + σElo(n)²) · √(2 ln N) (p. 68).

FIGURES: Figure 9, p. 14, "Allowing retraction of scores allows providers to skew Arena scores upwards." It shows identical checkpoints at 1069 vs 1052 with other models ranked between them, which makes rank noise visible at a glance. Alternative: Figure 7, p. 12 (best score vs number of variants).

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions addressed to the reader. The de-anonymising prompts on p. 47 are quoted study material.
- Internal inconsistency: the Section 3 findings box (p. 10) says "testing just 10 variants yields a notable increase of approximately 100 points", while the body (p. 13) and Appendix I say about 50 points at 20 variants. Use the body figure.
- Dataset size is stated variously as 1.8M (p. 44), 1.9M (Table 1) and "around 2M" (p. 46).
- "grown by 20%" for multilingual share means points (23.9% to 43.5%).
- Extraction: frequent missing spaces, equations and Table 1 icons garbled, figure axis values interleaved with text. Numbers quoted above come from prose or captions.
